newsitem.title: JAPAN: Mergers remain popular as corporate Japan regroups.
newsitem.headline: Mergers remain popular as corporate Japan regroups.

text.p: The urge to merge remained strong in corporate Japan during the last business year, as companies restructured their businesses and scouted around for allies to sharpen competitiveness at home and abroad.

Japan's anti-monopoly watchdog said on Tuesday that it received a total of 2,271 merger filings in the fiscal year to the end of March, the second-largest number on record following the previous year's 2,520 cases.
"My impression is that some mergers were carried out in the face of the increasing need to restructure operations within the same corporate groups," a Fair Trade Commission (FTC) official said.

Although hardly signalling a U.S.-style merger boom, the figures show how deregulation, cost-cutting pressures and the need to compete in overseas markets are increasingly forcing Japanese companies to regroup and form strategic alliances.

The official declined to comment on whether the current merger trend is likelyto persist, but he added that the recent scrapping of a 50-year-old ban on holding companies would give companies more options in their much-needed restructuring.
Of the total mergers, nearly half were small in scale, the FTC said in a report.

It said there were 1,048 mergers with combined assets of less than one billion yen ($8.8 million), or 46.1 percent of the total number, down from 1,385 the year before. Large-scale mergers involving combined assets of 50 billion yen ($442 million) or more totalled 82, up from 80 the previous year.

The number of business transfers, typically the takeover of operations at a troubled affiliate, also hit a record of 1,476 in 1996/97 compared with 1,467 the previous year, suggesting that the growth trend remains intact, the FTC said.

Despite the growing number of corporate courtships, Japan continues to lag far behind the United States, where telecommunications, utilities and insurance companies have led a nearly two-year-old merger boom.

The driving force for the U.S. merger mania has been the U.S. stock market, coupled with trends toward consolidation and cost-cutting that have helped corporate America strengthen its international position.
The number of Japanese mergers has also been boosted by a change in the law which stipulates that companies must have capital of at least 10 million yen ($88,400), the FTC official said.
Among the merger filings was an alliance between two paperboard producers and a tie-up by chemical makers, all struggling to survive tough global competition.
In February, Japan Paper Industry Co Ltd announced plans to merge in October with Jujo Paper Board Co Ltd. Both firms are members of the large Nippon Paper Industries Co Ltd group.
Analysts say the merger, aimed at cutting costs by streamlining manufacturing and supply channels, could trigger an overhaul of the nation's crowded paper industry.

In October, Mitsui Toatsu Chemicals Inc and Mitsui Petrochemical Industries Ltd, both in the Mitsui group, said they would merge later this year to become the nation's second-biggest chemical maker. The action was aimed at boosting competitiveness in the global chemical market.
Companies must file merger plans with the FTC under Japan's anti-monopoly law, although not all such plans bear fruit.

Last month, Sega Enterprises Ltd and Bandai Co Ltd abruptly called off a much-trumpeted merger that would have created Japan's largest game company. The cancellation came only a day before the two firms were due to approve a merger pact and was prompted by strong opposition to the alliance from mid-level Bandai managers. ($1=113 yen)
